experiments.title: The 20 most recent posts by one user
experiments.question:
The profile page: the latest 20 posts by one user, newest first. The user picked is the
most prolific author on the site (4,428 posts), which is the worst case for this page.

variants.name: index on (owner_user_id)
variants.note: Finds the rows for the user through the index, but still fetches and sorts all of them to keep 20.

variants.name: index on (owner_user_id, creation_date DESC, id DESC)
variants.note: The index is already in the order the page wants, so the scan stops after 20 entries and nothing is sorted.

experiments.title: The 50 newest questions with a given tag
experiments.question:
Tags arrive in the dump as one string per question, `|bash|scripts|`. The loader also
splits them into a `post_tags (post_id, tag_id)` table. Which shape answers "newest 50
questions tagged bash" fastest, and does the junction table's primary key help?

variants.name: junction table, primary key (post_id, tag_id) only
variants.note: The key starts with post_id, so it cannot be used to look up a tag: the whole junction table is read.

variants.name: trigram index on the tag string
variants.note: Keeps the original LIKE query unchanged; costs a much larger index.

variants.name: junction table carrying creation_date, index on (tag_id, creation_date DESC, post_id DESC)
variants.note: Every earlier variant must fetch all 11,211 bash questions to find the newest 50. Copying the (immutable) creation date into the junction row lets the index hand back the newest 50 directly.

experiments.title: Page 4,001 of the question list
experiments.question:
Questions newest first, 50 per page. Both variants have the same index on
(creation_date, id); the only difference is how the page is addressed. OFFSET has to
walk past every earlier row; keyset pagination starts from the last row of the
previous page.

experiments.title: Up-votes per day over the last month
experiments.question:
A dashboard query over the biggest table (4.9M votes): up-votes per day since
1 March 2024. Five ways to index a date range, with what each index costs on disk.

variants.name: BRIN on (creation_date)
variants.note: A BRIN index stores one min/max per range of pages. Votes.xml is not in id or date order (physical correlation 0.61), so recent votes sit in 24% of the pages, spread across every range: the index rules nothing out, and the scan it produces is not parallel.

variants.name: BRIN on (creation_date), on a copy of the table stored in date order
variants.note: Same rows, same kind of index, 48 kB. The only change is the physical order of the rows.

variants.name: B-tree on (creation_date, vote_type_id)
variants.note: Both columns the query needs are in the index, so the table itself is never read (index-only scan).

experiments.title: Find a user by name, ignoring case
experiments.question:
Wrapping a column in a function hides it from an ordinary index. Looking up a display
name with lower() across 1.48M users: no index, an index on the column, and an index on
the expression.

variants.name: index on (display_name)
variants.note: Built, paid for, and not used: the index is on display_name, the query filters on lower(display_name).

experiments.title: Users who have never posted
experiments.question:
Three ways to write an anti-join. 16,835 posts have no owner (the account was deleted),
so the sub-select contains NULLs. `x NOT IN (..., NULL)` is never true, so the obvious
NOT IN query returns zero users instead of 1.16 million, and at the default work_mem
it does not even finish.

variants.name: NOT IN, default work_mem (4MB)
variants.note: The id list does not fit in work_mem, so Postgres re-scans it for every user: about 1.5M x 0.9M comparisons. Cancelled at the time limit.

variants.name: NOT IN, work_mem 256MB
variants.note: Now it finishes, with the wrong answer: 0. One NULL in the list makes NOT IN unknown for every row.

variants.name: NOT IN with NULLs filtered, work_mem 256MB

experiments.title: The best answer to each question asked last month
experiments.question:
Greatest-one-per-group: for each question asked in March 2024, its highest-scored
answer. Three ways to write it, tried without and with an index on
(parent_id, score DESC, id). Every variant has the same index for finding the
questions of the month, so only the per-question lookup differs.

variants.name: LATERAL, no index
variants.note: One full scan of posts per question. Cancelled at the time limit.

experiments.title: Search question titles

variants.name: ILIKE + B-tree on (title)
variants.note: Not used: a pattern that starts with % has no prefix to search the B-tree with.

variants.name: full-text search + GIN on to_tsvector(title)
variants.note: Matches the words in any order and any form (driver, drivers), and treats nvidia-driver-535 as separate words, so the row set differs on purpose.

experiments.title: Delete five posts
experiments.question:
Postgres indexes the referenced side of a foreign key (it must be a primary key or
unique) but not the referencing side. Deleting a post makes it check every table that
points at posts: comments, votes, post_links (twice) and posts itself (parent_id,
accepted_answer_id). Without an index on those columns each check is a full scan, once
per deleted row. The five posts chosen have nothing pointing at them, so the delete is
legal; it runs inside a transaction that is rolled back.

variants.name: referencing columns not indexed
variants.note: The plan for the DELETE itself is trivial; the time is in the foreign-key triggers, which the buffer count does not include.

experiments.title: Posts per holder of one gold badge
experiments.question:
The planner multiplies the selectivity of each filter as if columns were independent.
A badge name fixes its class ("Famous Question" is always gold), so
`name = 'Famous Question' AND class = 1` is estimated as 2% x 2.4% of badges when the
truth is 2%. Extended statistics on (name, class) tell the planner about the
dependency. Does the better estimate change the plan, and the time?

experiments.title: The date of the latest vote of one type
experiments.question:
An index is not always the faster path. Vote type 2 (up-vote) is 73% of the table;
type 7 (reopen) is 198 rows. The same index on (vote_type_id) is offered for both.
For the common value the planner ignores it; forcing it shows the planner was right.
The last two variants ask about the rare value, so they return a different row and
their times should be compared with each other, not with the first variant.

variants.name: common value, index on (vote_type_id) available
variants.note: The index exists and the planner still reads the whole table.

experiments.title: Insert 200,000 votes
experiments.question:
Every index in the other experiments makes a read faster. This is the bill. The same
200,000 rows are inserted into a 1,000,000-row copy of votes carrying 0, 1, 3 and 6
indexes. The copy is rebuilt for every variant and each insert is rolled back.
